P10n: Most institutions get more and more layers and offices as they age. The Zapatistas did a review of theirs, and then pushed authority down. Did they put out a book on leadership and open a certification program? No, they changed the system they were actually living in.

P13o: They're also not proof of my whole economic path, the one that goes from unpriced internal necessities, to a common purse, to getting rid of outside money. Zapatista communities use collective work to support their schools and clinics, and their autonomous government and their resistance. But they also sell products and trade, and they get support from outside. What they do show is that a community can stop buying major necessities and public functions on the market, and govern them collectively instead. Help from outside can make a community more capable. But it can also create gatekeepers and uneven dependence, if the specialist or the donor or the organization stays indispensable.

P16a2: In my research I also looked into what came out of the Escuelita. There are alumni networks, and people took practices home and organized later. But I couldn't find a clean chain from one Escuelita student to a new communal institution, with evidence of how its members and their kids actually did over time. And Zapatista influence was spreading internationally before the Escuelita, so a later resemblance alone doesn't prove it came from there. So I'm borrowing a way of teaching and the ambition to replicate. I'm not claiming the Zapatistas already proved my whole model.

P17f: Sociocracy has a very different history, but some similar forms: circles, consent, distributed authority, and links between levels. That doesn't prove there's a universal formula. But it gives builders another serious system to study, so they don't have to invent their governance on the fly during their first dispute.
